answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This is a genuine Paine line. It appears in the Introduction to Common Sense (first published 10 January 1776), and the popular wording matches the pamphlet verbatim: “a long habit of not thinking a thing wrong, gives it a superficial appearance of being right.” Confirmed against the full text.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: Perhaps the sentiments contained in the following pages, are not YET sufficiently fashionable to procure them general favour; a long habit of not thinking a thing wrong, gives it a superficial appearance of being right, and raises at first a formidable outcry in defence of custom. But the tumult soon subsides.
trail: The line appears in the Introduction to Common Sense on ushistory.org, matching the popular wording exactly.
It is independently confirmed in the pamphlet text hosted by the Thomas Paine National Historical Association.
Both texts date the pamphlet’s first publication to 10 January 1776, placing the work firmly in the public domain.
source.excerptNote: The famous line opens the pamphlet’s Introduction, where Paine warns that custom is often mistaken for correctness.

author.name: Thomas Paine
author.heading: About Thomas Paine
author.bio: Thomas Paine was a radical pamphleteer whose plain, forceful prose helped ignite the American Revolution. Common Sense (1776) sold in the hundreds of thousands and made the case for independence to ordinary colonists; he followed it with The American Crisis, Rights of Man, and The Age of Reason. He is one of the internet’s most fabricated-for names — which makes a genuinely sourced line like this one worth flagging.

misattribution.heading: Is it really Paine?
misattribution.intro: Thomas Paine is a magnet for invented quotations, so skepticism is the right default. This one, however, is authentic — the caution is about wording, not authorship.

items.why: The line is sometimes rendered as “a long habit of not thinking a thing is wrong” or with modernized punctuation. Paine’s original reads “a long habit of not thinking a thing wrong, gives it a superficial appearance of being right” — verified in the Introduction to Common Sense.
The quote circulates widely on quote sites and social media with no citation, which fuels doubt. In this case the source is real and specific: the opening pages of Common Sense.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuine Paine: the sentence appears verbatim in the Introduction to Common Sense (1776).

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Paine placed this line at the very start of Common Sense to disarm readers before making his radical argument for independence. He anticipates that his ideas will meet resistance — not because they are wrong, but because monarchy and colonial loyalty had become customary and therefore felt right.
The sentence has since become a general-purpose aphorism about how habit launders bad ideas into respectable ones, quoted far beyond its revolutionary origins.
context.pull: Time makes more converts than reason.
